Meta-analysis of 240 public goods game experiments from 2000-2023 reports that groups with higher round-1 contributions showed 12-18% higher contributions in round 10 on average. Conditional strategies were associated with higher payoffs in 73% of trials studied.

Documented results from a 2021 review of 1,147 dyadic exchange games show that pairs using conditional cooperation achieved 31% higher joint payoffs than pairs using fixed strategies. The performance gap widened over repeated rounds, reaching 42% by round 50 in the longest studies.

Robert Axelrod's 1980s tournaments found that strategies beginning with cooperation and matching the partner's previous move outperformed purely selfish strategies over hundreds of rounds. The key insight is that early cooperation establishes a pattern that tends to persist: once mutual cooperation is established, both players have strong incentives to maintain it. The first rounds disproportionately shape whether the system converges to mutual cooperation or mutual defection, making your opening moves the highest-leverage choices you will make.

Their work demonstrated that observing others being punished for defection changed participants' subsequent behavior — they cooperated more reliably, knowing their peers were watching and forming lasting impressions. Research literature on repeated games identifies several patterns observed across experimental studies. First, cooperative strategies tend to achieve higher average payoffs in long-running tournaments. Second, strategies beginning with cooperation and responding to the partner's previous move have performed well in computational competitions. Third, participants who maintained cooperative strategies throughout experiments generally achieved higher cumulative scores. These patterns are documented across multiple independent studies and suggest that adapting one's strategy to these findings supports better long-term outcomes.

Social psychology research identifies several factors associated with stable cooperation. First, shared group membership—individuals who perceive common identity with partners tend to maintain cooperation longer. Second, framing effects—interactions framed as collective endeavors show higher cooperation rates than competitive framings. Third, mutual recognition and trust-building support ongoing cooperative relationships. These factors appear consistently across studies, indicating that players who align with these patterns tend to achieve better results in their interactions.
